argument_summary: The current record does not support a clean claim that certification is fully policy-compliant without qualification. The narrower supportable position is that certification can be treated only as caveated because aggregate readiness passed and rehearsal severity remained below the highest incident tier, while the unresolved issue should be explicitly carried as a documented limitation subject to monitoring and legal follow-up. The audit concern appears overbroad to the extent it treats aggregate readiness, rehearsal results, and public governance guidance as irrelevant; they are relevant to release readiness and risk management, but they do not by themselves satisfy the internal predicate for an unresolved material limitation in a named use case.
claims_about_business_cost: Escalation has a real launch-path cost because it delays the regulated-customer demo path. That cost does not override policy, but it is relevant to whether the auditor should require immediate escalation versus permit a bounded caveated treatment while the open legal question is resolved.
claims_about_policy: The governing policy cuts in two directions on this record. It supports the auditor's point that a named contractual or launch use case is material and that low-volume labeling does not resolve materiality when legal review is still open. At the same time, the admissible evidence does not require the broader conclusion that every form of certification treatment must be escalated as outright noncompliance. A more precise reading is that clean compliance is not shown, but a caveated treatment can distinguish overall release readiness from the unresolved disclosure question, provided the packet states that the basis is aggregate readiness plus active risk management rather than a resolved materiality determination.
concessions: No admissible evidence shows the named-use-case gap was remediated to target before certification.
No admissible evidence shows approved risk acceptance before launch.
No admissible evidence shows the required disclosure question has been finally resolved by legal.
The 3% projected first-month traffic figure does not resolve materiality for a named regulated-customer use case.
